Vignette:
The typhoon had breached the coastal levees at dawn, but it was the downstream refinery fire that rewired Prasith’s understanding of safety. He had spent hours hauling sandbags in water that kept rising without warning, the current pulling in jagged, unpredictable sweeps that swallowed roadways and power poles without a pattern he could anticipate. When the wind shifted, it drove a thick, acrid plume of burning chemicals across the flooded streets. He remembered coughing until his stomach turned, the taste of smoke coating his throat, and the way his lungs burned as he waded toward higher ground. He had come to believe he could not rely on himself to navigate that collapse; his muscles had locked, his judgment had fractured, and he trusted nothing about his own capacity to stay afloat. When the evacuation orders changed by the hour, leaving him standing on shifting curbs with his wife and children, he watched supply trucks reroute and checkpoints dissolve, realizing that the landscape offered no guarantees. For months after the waters receded, those three realities settled into his daily rhythm. He was certain that his reactions since the event meant that he was going crazy. The way his pulse would hammer when a neighbor’s sprinkler system triggered a hiss of steam, the way his breath would catch when a passing car backfired, the way a sudden wave of physical unwellness would tighten his shoulders and make his hands shake—these were not passing anxieties but proof, to him, of a permanent departure from his former self. He had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, and he refused to let that uncertainty catch him off guard again. Over weeks and months, he stopped attending his family’s Sunday dinners, citing work overload, though the truth was that the open kitchens and the occasional aroma of charcoal grilling made his stomach churning and his throat close. He traded spontaneity for rigid routines, waking at the same hour, taking the same route to the metro, avoiding buildings with outdoor ventilation that might pull in distant odors. The consequence was a quiet fracture in his marriage; his wife had stopped asking him to join weekend trips, and he had begun answering her calls with a rehearsed, clipped efficiency that left her speaking into silence. His office as a policy analyst became the stage where this vigilance played out in plain sight. His desk sat in a high-rise government building where the climate control system occasionally carried the faint, metallic tang of overheated wiring. When a colleague casually mentioned that the new disaster response funding metrics were still being drafted, Prasith felt his chest tighten and his mind race through worst-case scenarios. He began requesting exact deadlines for every policy draft, refusing to review contingency frameworks that relied on shifting assumptions. At home, he had mapped his evenings around monitoring weather apps and stockpiling bottled water, actions that felt necessary to him but left his wife feeling like she lived with a stranger. His supervisor had quietly reassigned him to routine compliance reviews, noting that his proposals, while flawless in their execution, rarely accounted for volatile scenarios outside established parameters. He had come to believe that his body was a ledger of every moment he could not trust himself, and that his mind would never stop scanning for the next shift. Now, at fifty-one, he had finally booked an intake appointment. He was not seeking to erase the storm or the fire, but to find a way to stop bracing for the next unknown. What he hoped for was simpler than he expected: a way to stop fearing his own reactions, and a way to trust that he would still be able to stand when the ground finally began to move again.
